question:
Which of the below has not undergone trisyllabic laxing during its sound development: 

southern, derivative, serenity, pleasant, gratitude, shadow

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The three polysyllabic items in the list are the ones that show the
normal English trisyllabic shortening/laxing of a stem vowel before an
additional unstressed syllable.

* derivative < deriv-  /dɪˈraɪv/ > /dɪˈrɪvə-/
* serenity < serene /səˈriːn/ > /səˈrɛnə-/
* gratitude < grate /ɡreɪt/ > /ˈɡrætɪ-/ 

are all ≥3-syllable formations in which the stressed stem vowel is
phonologically laxed / shortened with respect to the bisyllabic stem.
Southern is the textbook disyllabic counterexample, /ˈsaʊðən/ ~ /ˈsʌðən/,
and it never had a trisyllabic base to condition a trisyllabic shortening.
In the same formal class pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ and shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ are also
only disyllabic and therefore can have no trisyllabic laxing in their
development, the same formal point that is normally illustrated with
southern.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: shadow

The three uncontroversial Latinate trisyllabic laxing cases in the set are
derivative ∼ derive, serenity ∼ serene and gratitude ∼ grate.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪvə tɪv/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛnə ti/
* grate /ɡreɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡrætɪ tjʊd/

In each case a tense stressed vowel of the disyllabic base is laxed /
shortened when it is followed by two unstressed syllables in the derived
form, the classic penultimate-stress / initial-stress trisyllabic laxing
environment.

southern /ˈsʌðən/ and pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ are disyllabic in present-day
English and cannot in principle show trisyllabic laxing; pleasant
/ˈplɛzənt/ ∼ please /pliːz/ is the ordinary -ant / -ent disyllabic
laxing / *pleas*ant.

shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/ is the clear non-Latinate, essentially disyllabic
Germanic item.  Its /æ/ goes back to OE sceadu < *skadw- and the
shade /eɪ/ > shadow /æ/ change is regular Middle English vowel
development before a voiced stop / *o* vocalisation, not the
post-Latinate trisyllabic environment that produces /aɪ/ > /ɪ/, /iː/ >
/e/ ~ /ɛ/ and /eɪ/ > /æ/ in three-syllable Latinate derivatives. In
the ordinary textbook set the Germanic disyllabic shadow is the item
that is not a trisyllabic laxing derivative at all.  Southern and
pleasant are the other disyllabic non-trisyllabic cases.

5.text:
Trisyllabic shortening / laxing is the English historical/phonological
shortening of a root long vowel when the root is extended by a
post-tonic suffix so that the vowel comes to be in a stressed syllable
of a word of three or more syllables. The classic environment is

   long vowel → lax/short vowel / _ ]σ σσ

e.g.

* derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > derivative /dɪˈrɪv.ə.tɪv/   /aɪ/ > /ɪ/
* serene /səˈriːn/ > serenity /səˈrɛ.nɪ.ti/   /iː/ > /ɛ/
* please /pliːz/ > pleasant /ˈplɛz.ənt/ ,
* grate /greɪt/ > gratitude /ˈɡræ.tɪ.tuːd/   /eɪ/ > /æ/

i.e. a long stressed vowel of the base is laxed/shortened in the
polysyllabic derivative. The same root-and-suffix history is what is
normally quoted for serenity, derivative, gratitude and, in the
text-book sense, pleasant.

Shadow /ˈʃæ.doʊ/ < OE *sceadu, ME shade /ʃeɪd/ is a simple
disyllabic nominal formation. Its /eɪ/ > /æ/ change is the regular
Middle-English lowering /eɪ/ > /æ/ before a post-vocalic /ʊ/ /oʊ/ and
has nothing to do with the addition of a post-tonic suffix which
makes the word trisyllabic. It is for that reason the clear non-member
of the set. 

In strict syllable-count terms southern /ˈsʌð.ən/ and pleasant
/ˈplɛz.ənt/ are likewise bisyllabic and therefore cannot be a
text-book case of trisyllabic laxing; shadow is the usual textbook
odd-man-out in the list given.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I would select **shadow**. Its /æ/ does not reflect a long vowel that was shortened by trisyllabic laxing; it descends from the Old English vowel/diphthong in *sceadu/sceadwe*, which was already short/non-long in the relevant environment, and the modern word does not show the typical TSL pattern in the same way. The other items show the expected long-to-short alternation in a trisyllabic or derived environment: *serene/serenity*, *derive/derivative*, *grateful/gratitude*, *south/southern*, and *pleasant* (with its shortened vowel in the derived/borrowed form). So **shadow** is the outlier.

before a second unstressed syllable; the /æ/ goes back to the Old English

has undergone the regular Great Vowel Shift development of that root.

Core laxing cases that are undisputed:
* derivative < derive /dɪˈraɪv/ > /dɪˈrɪvətɪv/  /aɪ/ → /ɪ/
* serenity < serene /səˈriːn/ > /səˈrɛnəti/  /iː/ → /ɛ/
* gratitude < grate /greɪt/ > /ˈɡrætıtuːd/  /eɪ/ → /æ/
All three are classic Latinate post-tonic suffixation examples with a tense stem vowel laxed/shortened in a polysyllabic derivative.

Disyllabic/non-trisyllabic items:
* southern /ˈsʌðən/ < south. Disyllabic today, no trisyllabic base to condition trisyllabic shortening. Cited as textbook disyllabic counterexample.
* pleasant /ˈplɛzənt/ < please /pliːz/. Present-day disyllabic. Colleagues split on label: Colleague2 and Colleague5 treat it as a textbook laxing example in the loose sense please → pleasant; Colleague1,3 treat it as ordinary disyllabic -ant/-ent laxing, not true trisyllabic laxing. Strict syllable-count definition would exclude it.
* shadow /ˈʃædoʊ/. Native Germanic < OE sceadu. /æ/ reflects OE ea, not a historically long vowel shortened by post-Latinate suffixation. Regular Middle English lowering /eɪ/ > /æ/ before post-vocalic /ʊ/~/oʊ/ in the shade/shadow relationship; no suffix-driven trisyllabic environment ever. Disyllabic always.

Unresolved nuance: strict definition requires the stressed vowel to be in a word of three or more syllables with two following unstressed syllables. Under that strict count, pleasant and southern are bisyllabic now and cannot be textbook trisyllabic laxing; gratitude is the only first-stressed trisyllabic example in the list, with derivative and serenity being penultimate-stressed polysyllabic laxing.

Consensus emerging in round 0: shadow is the clear non-member of the set because its vowel development is Germanic historical lowering, not post-Latinate trisyllabic shortening/laxing.
